main.title: World's Columbian Exposition
main.summary: The World's Columbian Exposition, also known as the Chicago World's Fair, was a world's fair held in Chicago from May 1 to October 30, 1893, to celebrate the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus's arrival in the New World in 1492.

cards.heading: World's Columbian Exposition
cards.text:
The World's Columbian Exposition, also known as the Chicago World's Fair, was a world's fair held in Chicago from May 1 to October 30, 1893, to celebrate the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus's arrival in the New World in 1492. The centerpiece of the fair, held in Jackson Park, was a large water pool representing the voyage that Columbus took to the New World. Chicago won the right to host the fair over several competing cities, including New York City, Washington, D.C., and St. Louis. The exposition was an influential social and cultural event and had a profound effect on American architecture, the arts, American industrial optimism, and Chicago's image.

A highlight was that Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse showcased their alternating current (AC) system, effectively winning the war of the currents against Thomas Edison's direct current (DC). The fair was the first all-electric, featuring over 200,000 lamps powered by Tesla's polyphase system, demonstrating its superior safety and efficiency for long-distance power distribution.

main.title: The Lumière brothers: the Cinématographe screenings
main.summary: In 1895, Auguste and Louis Lumière demonstrated the Cinématographe and held their first commercial public screening in Paris on 28 December.

cards.heading: The Lumière brothers: the Cinématographe screenings
cards.text:
In 1895, Auguste and Louis Lumière demonstrated the Cinématographe and held their first commercial public screening in Paris on 28 December.

The Lumière brothers, Auguste Marie Louis Nicolas Lumière (19 October 1862 – 10 April 1954) and Louis Jean Lumière (5 October 1864 – 6 June 1948), were French manufacturers of photography equipment, best known for their Cinématographe motion picture system and the short films they produced between 1895 and 1905, which places them among the earliest filmmakers.

Their screening of a single film on 22 March 1895, for around 200 members of the Société d'encouragement pour l'industrie nationale (Society for the Development of the National Industry) in Paris was probably the first presentation of projected film. Their first commercial public screening on 28 December 1895, for around 40 paying visitors and invited relations, has traditionally been regarded as the birth of cinema.

main.title: X-ray
main.summary: An X-ray is a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength shorter than those of ultraviolet rays and longer than those of gamma rays.

cards.heading: X-ray
cards.text:
An X-ray is a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength shorter than those of ultraviolet rays and longer than those of gamma rays. Roughly, X-rays have a wavelength ranging from 10 nanometers to 10 picometers, corresponding to frequencies in the range of 30 petahertz to 30 exahertz (3×1016 Hz to 3×1019 Hz) and photon energies in the range of 100 eV to 100 keV, respectively.

X-rays were discovered in 1895 by the German scientist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who named it X-radiation to signify an unknown type of radiation.

X-rays can penetrate many solid substances such as construction materials and living tissue, so X-ray radiography is widely used in medical diagnostics (e.g., checking for broken bones) and materials science (e.g., identification of some chemical elements and detecting weak points in construction materials). However X-rays are ionizing radiation and exposure can be hazardous to health, causing DNA damage, cancer and, at higher intensities, burns and radiation sickness. Their generation and use is strictly controlled by public health authorities.

main.title: Athens 1896 Olympics
main.summary: Athens hosted the first modern Olympic Games from 6 to 15 April 1896.

cards.heading: Athens 1896 Olympics
cards.text: Athens hosted the first modern Olympic Games from 6 to 15 April 1896. Organised by the International Olympic Committee established by Pierre de Coubertin, they brought together athletes from fourteen countries according to the IOC's count. All competitors were men, and most were Greek. Winners received silver medals and runners-up copper, before the IOC later assigned the familiar gold, silver and bronze rankings retrospectively. American triple jumper James Connolly became the first Olympic medallist in more than fifteen centuries on the opening day.

main.title: Becquerel discovers radioactivity
main.summary: Henri Becquerel observed spontaneous radiation from uranium minerals in 1896.

cards.heading: Becquerel discovers radioactivity
cards.text: Henri Becquerel observed spontaneous radiation from uranium minerals in 1896. Certain materials were releasing energy through changes inside their atoms, opening a new field of investigation. Radioactive decay occurs when an unstable nucleus loses energy, commonly through alpha, beta or gamma radiation. The moment a particular atom will decay cannot be predicted, but large groups have measurable rates expressed through a half-life. Those periods vary enormously between isotopes, from almost instantaneous changes to times longer than the age of the universe.

main.title: Braun develops the cathode-ray tube
main.summary: Karl Ferdinand Braun developed his cathode-ray tube in 1897.

cards.heading: Braun develops the cathode-ray tube
cards.text: Karl Ferdinand Braun developed his cathode-ray tube in 1897. Inside a vacuum tube, an electron beam could be directed towards a phosphorescent screen, which emitted light where the beam struck. This made electrical signals visible and supplied a principle later used in oscilloscopes, television sets and computer monitors. Electrodes focused the electrons, while coils or plates steered their path. By controlling where the beam landed, the tube could turn an electrical process into a waveform, a moving image or a computer display.

main.title: Thomson identifies the electron
main.summary: J. J. Thomson's cathode-ray experiments in 1897 identified the electron as a particle smaller than an atom.

cards.heading: Thomson identifies the electron
cards.text: J. J. Thomson's cathode-ray experiments in 1897 identified the electron as a particle smaller than an atom. Work involving John Townsend and Charles Wilson changed the understanding of matter's structure. Electrons carry a negative charge and have far less mass than protons or neutrons. Their arrangement around an atomic nucleus helps determine a substance's chemical properties. The outer electrons can be transferred or shared between atoms, forming the bonds of molecules and crystals. A discovery within a laboratory tube therefore reached into explanations of ordinary materials and chemical reactions.

main.title: Marie Curie: polonium and radium
main.summary: In 1898, Marie and Pierre Curie announced polonium and radium, opening a new stage in the study of radioactivity.

cards.heading: Marie Curie: polonium and radium
cards.text: In July 1898, Marie and Pierre Curie announced evidence of a new element, which they named polonium after Marie’s native Poland. In December, working with Gustave Bémont, they announced a second strongly radioactive substance and proposed the name radium. These announcements established the discoveries; separating the elements in quantities sufficient for detailed study required further years of work.

main.title: Planck's law
main.summary: In 1900, Max Planck developed a formula to explain the observed spectrum of radiation from a body in thermal equilibrium.

cards.heading: Planck's law
cards.text: In 1900, Max Planck developed a formula to explain the observed spectrum of radiation from a body in thermal equilibrium. Existing theories diverged from measurements at high frequencies. Planck proposed that an oscillator could change its energy only in discrete increments proportional to frequency. He initially treated this as a mathematical device for obtaining the right result. Other physicists, including Einstein, developed the idea further. What began as a solution to a particular radiation problem became a fundamental contribution to quantum theory.

main.title: Marconi: a wireless signal across the Atlantic
main.summary: In December 1901, Guglielmo Marconi reported receiving a wireless signal sent from Cornwall to Newfoundland.

cards.heading: Marconi: a wireless signal across the Atlantic
cards.text: On 12 December 1901, Guglielmo Marconi and his assistant George Kemp reported hearing the Morse letter S—three dots—at Signal Hill in St John’s, Newfoundland. The signal had been transmitted from Poldhu in Cornwall. The reported transatlantic reception became a landmark in long-distance wireless communication.
